case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that the Due Process Clause requires at least clear and convincing evidence before a State may terminate parental rights, vacated the judgment approving New York's preponderance standard, and left States free to adopt any burden at or above that level.
key_cases.relevance: This is the federal constitutional floor for the standard of proof in every termination of parental rights case, including Kansas proceedings under K.S.A. 38-2269.
key_cases.quote: due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence

key_cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that due process does not require appointment of counsel for indigent parents in every parental termination proceeding, leaving the decision in the first instance to the trial court applying the Mathews v. Eldridge factors subject to appellate review, and affirmed on the facts.
key_cases.relevance: This is the federal baseline on appointed counsel at termination; Kansas exceeds it by statute, and Kansas courts apply its Mathews framework to related counsel questions.
key_cases.quote: neither can we say that the Constitution requires the appointment of counsel in every parental termination proceeding

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed termination of parental rights, holding that appellate courts reviewing unfitness findings view all the evidence in the light most favorable to the State, ask only whether a rational factfinder could have found unfitness highly probable, and may not reweigh evidence or reassess witness credibility.
key_cases.relevance: This is the current Kansas Supreme Court statement of the appellate standard governing termination of parental rights, including the unfitness and foreseeable-future elements.
key_cases.quote: the appellate court does not weigh conflicting evidence, pass on the credibility of witnesses, or redetermine questions of fact

key_cases.holding: The court reversed a termination of parental rights, holding that a party who appears for a termination hearing is presumed to want to participate fully, that the district court must ensure the party can see, hear, speak and consult counsel, and that any waiver of that right must be knowing, voluntary, intelligent and on the record.
key_cases.relevance: This sets the current Kansas due process floor for the conduct of a termination hearing itself, independent of the sufficiency of the evidence.
key_cases.quote: a waiver of an appearing party's right to fully and meaningfully participate in a termination of parental rights hearing must be made knowingly, voluntarily, intelligently, and on the record

key_cases.case_name: In re Adoption of Baby Girl P.
key_cases.holding: The court reversed the termination of a natural father's parental rights and the Court of Appeals' affirmance, holding that the adoption petitioners failed to prove any K.S.A. 59-2136(h)(1) factor by clear and convincing evidence and that the child's best interests cannot alone justify termination, and remanded for a custodial transition to the father not to exceed 30 days.
key_cases.relevance: This is the Kansas Supreme Court's statement of the clear-and-convincing burden an adoption petitioner bears before a natural father's rights may be terminated.
key_cases.quote: As with stepparent adoptions, the best interest of the child may not be the sole basis for terminating a parent's rights

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed the district court's refusal to set aside a finalized adoption, holding that an unwed father of a newborn who did not grasp his fleeting opportunity to commit to parenting during the pregnancy acquired no protected liberty interest, so the absence of notice to him did not make the adoption void, and rejecting his fraud and equal protection theories.
key_cases.relevance: This is the leading Kansas authority on an unwed father's notice and consent rights when adoption is the permanency outcome, and on how quickly that opportunity closes.
key_cases.quote: We hold that M.P. did not have a liberty interest in a relationship with A.A.T. and that the State did not deny him the opportunity to establish such a relationship
